description: Team Northern Lights is a multidisciplinary squad of engineers, software developers, and planetary data enthusiasts. Inspired by NASA’s Artemis and SWIM initiatives, we bridge Earth observation and deep-space exploration to uncover and characterize ideal planetary analog sites for sustainable lunar and Martian habitats.
summary:
SolMate is an open web app that searches the whole land surface of Earth for places that behave like the Moon and Mars. It answers the challenge directly: it scores Earth against 11 NASA targets (the nine Artemis candidate regions at the lunar south pole, Jezero Crater and Arcadia Planitia) on seven characteristics, not just looks: terrain, climate and aridity, temperature, surface, mineralogy, ice and cold traps, and dust. Every number comes from NASA data, including ASTER, MODIS, NASA POWER, MERRA-2, LRO and Mars 2020. About 1.9 million places get a transparent 0-100 score, and any place a user clicks is scored live in the browser. Each result also says where the analogy breaks down (gravity, air pressure, radiation) and what the site could be used for.

Why it matters: today's analog sites are few and mostly chosen by eye. SolMate found 53 of its top 55 places more than 300 km from any known site, and a pre-registered test shows known NASA analogs outscore control sites (AUC 0.84 for Jezero). It gives mission planners a global shortlist, and students a Learn page and map game.
details:
THE PROBLEM

Before astronauts and rovers go to the Moon or Mars, NASA tests them in places on Earth that behave like those worlds. But only a few dozen analog sites are known, most were chosen by eye, and few are measured on more than how they look. No place on Earth matches everything, so the question is which place matches which characteristic, and where the match breaks down.

WHAT WE BUILT

SolMate is an open web app that searches the whole land surface of Earth for analogs of 11 NASA targets: the nine candidate Artemis landing regions near the lunar south pole, Jezero Crater (Mars 2020) and Arcadia Planitia (NASA's human-base ice target on Mars).

HOW IT WORKS

1. NASA data on every world. We built a global 0.1° stack of NASA Earth layers (about 1.9 million land cells) and a matching value for each target from NASA lunar and Mars data or cited mission results.

2. Seven characteristics. Terrain (ASTER GDEM v3, SRTMGL30), climate and aridity (NASA POWER), temperature (MODIS LST), surface (MODIS albedo and land cover), mineralogy (ASTER GED), ice and cold traps (MODIS snow; LRO LOLA, Diviner and illumination for the Moon) and dust (MERRA-2). Mars targets use Mars 2020 CTX, MOLA, MEDA, TES, CRISM and SWIM.

3. A transparent score. Each value is scored against Earth's own range: closeness when Earth can match the target, rank toward the target when it cannot, and the gap is stated. The dimensions combine into the SolMate Analog Index (SAI, 0-100). No AI model produces any number; the only fitted model is a cross-validated logistic regression for optional learned weights.

4. Two stages. The global screen ranks every cell; the leaders get 100 m NASA terrain.

5. Where it breaks down. Every result lists the gaps Earth cannot close (gravity, air pressure, radiation, extreme cold) and what the place could be used for: rover mobility, instrument tests, crew training or ice drilling rehearsals.

VALIDATION

The test was written down before it was run. Documented NASA analog sites outscore control sites (farmland, forest, cities, ice): AUC 0.84 for Jezero (95% CI 0.69-0.96) and a median of 0.76 for the nine Moon regions. Arcadia Planitia scores only 0.58, and we report that weak result rather than hide it. A high score marks a candidate for field review, not a proven analog.

FINDINGS

High, cold, barren plateaus are Earth's closest match to both worlds: 35 of the top 55 places lie on the Tibetan Plateau and 12 in the Puna de Atacama. 53 of those 55 are more than 300 km from all 31 known analog sites, so they are new leads. Two case studies: Jezero Crater and a Tibetan Plateau site (SAI 84.8), and Mons Mouton and a Pamir site (SAI 85.3). On event day we added NASA's LRO Diviner Polar Resource Product: within 1 m of the surface, water ice is stable over 11.5% to 72.6% of the Moon regions.

THE APP

- Explorer: pick a target, see Earth's best matches and novel leads, click any place to score it live in the browser.

- Twin Drive: drive a NASA rover over 20 km of real terrain on Earth and on Mars, side by side at the same scale.

- Place report: print any place as a PDF with scores, verdict and NASA images.

- Findings, Method and Data pages: the written report, how the score works, and every dataset with version and licence.

- Learn: six short levels for students aged 10-16, with an Analog Hunter game and quizzes.

It needs no login, works on phones, and the code is open source (Apache-2.0).

WHAT MAKES IT CREATIVE

- It looks beyond the famous sites: the whole planet is searched, and 53 of the top 55 places are new leads.

- It compares worlds on physics, not on pictures: seven measured characteristics instead of image similarity.

- It is honest about limits: every result says where Earth cannot match the target.

- Twin Drive lets anyone feel the analogy by driving the same rover on Earth and on Mars at the same scale.

TOOLS WE USED

- Science pipeline: Python (NumPy, SciPy, xarray, Zarr, rasterio, pyproj, pyhdf), packaged with uv and tested with pytest.

- Web app: TypeScript, React, Vite, Tailwind CSS, MapLibre GL for maps, three.js (React Three Fiber) for 3D terrain; scoring runs in a Web Worker in the browser.

- Cloud: Firebase Hosting; a small FastAPI terrain service on Google Cloud Run with Firebase App Check; Firestore.

- Quality and security: GitHub Actions CI, Playwright and axe accessibility tests, CodeQL, gitleaks secret scanning, Conventional Commits.

- No special hardware: everything runs on laptops and a low-cost cloud setup.

FACTORS WE CONSIDERED

- Scientific validity: a test written before it was run, confidence intervals, and weak results reported.

- NASA data first: every score uses NASA datasets; non-NASA data is optional and labelled.

- Cost and speed: most scoring runs in the user's browser, so it is instant and cheap to keep online.

- Access: no login, works on phones, keyboard and screen-reader friendly, open source under Apache-2.0.

- Security and privacy: no secrets in the code, no tracking, strict security headers.

USE OF AI

- No AI model produces any score or number: every result comes from deterministic code applied to NASA data.

- Code: the team designed SolMate and set every rule. Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic, in Claude Code) wrote most of the code, tests and docs under our direction, and GPT 6 Astra gave a second code review. The team checked every change before release.

- Research: Perplexity helped us find sources; every value is taken from the NASA product or the paper itself.

- Videos: the scenes are code written with Claude and rendered with HyperFrames, using real NASA footage, NASA data and screen captures of our app. There are no AI-generated images or video clips. Some voice lines are AI voice clones of our own voices (Cartesia, ElevenLabs); the end card and the YouTube description say so. Whisper timed the captions.

- Full list of tools: docs/AI_USE.md in the repository.

WHO IT HELPS

Analog mission planners, field geologists, rover and instrument test teams, and teachers and students.

WHAT'S NEXT

Field checks of the top new leads with geologists and analog teams, finer grids with more computing power, higher-resolution NASA data for targets with few known analogs, and NASA VIIRS data to replace MODIS when MODIS retires.

Live app: https://solmate-analog.web.app

Code: https://github.com/Tanbin-CS/solmate

Video (30 s): https://youtu.be/QA4dqsoJHYo
